title: CCSP (2026 outline) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from ISC2's public CCSP exam outline (effective Aug 1, 2026). Not real exam questions. The real CCSP is adaptive (100-150 items in 3 hours, multiple choice and advanced item types); this is a fixed 125-item stand-in with 4 advanced items.

q.q: A company buys cloud services through a firm that picks providers, negotiates contracts and combines several services for it. What role does that firm play?
o: Cloud service broker
Right. A broker sits between customers and providers and manages or combines services.
Cloud service provider
The firm isn't running the infrastructure itself.
Cloud auditor
Auditors assess. They don't buy or combine services.
Cloud carrier
A carrier provides connectivity, not service brokering.

q.q: Which cloud characteristic means the customer pays only for what it actually uses, tracked by the provider?
o: Measured service
Right. Usage is metered and billed.
Broad network access
That's about access, not billing.
Resource pooling
Pooling is about shared resources.
On-demand self-service
That's about provisioning without help.

q.q: Why is multitenancy a security concern in public cloud?
o: Tenants share hardware, so isolation between them must hold
Right. A flaw in isolation could let one tenant reach another's data.
Each tenant gets its own physical data center building
That isn't how public cloud works.
Tenants are never allowed to use encryption on shared hardware
Tenants can and should encrypt.
Multitenancy only applies to private clouds run in-house
It's a defining trait of public cloud.

q.q: A startup can launch servers in minutes during a demo and remove them an hour later. Which two characteristics make this possible?
o: On-demand self-service and rapid elasticity
Right. Users provision themselves, and capacity scales up and down quickly.
Measured service and data sovereignty
Billing and law don't make launching fast.
Resource pooling and long-term reserved contracts
Long contracts are the opposite of quick scaling.
Broad network access and physical tenant isolation
Neither explains the quick scale up and down.

q.q: A customer uploads code, and the provider runs it only when an event fires, managing all servers. Which model is this?
o: Function as a Service (serverless)
Right. The provider runs the code on demand and handles everything under it.
Infrastructure as a Service with customer-managed VMs
With IaaS the customer manages the OS.
Software as a Service with a finished application
SaaS is a finished app, not customer code.
A private cloud the customer runs on its own hardware
That isn't a provider-managed service.

q.q: A company wants to be able to move its workloads to a different cloud provider later without rewriting them. Which property matters MOST?
o: Portability
Right. Portability is the ability to move applications and data between providers.
Interoperability
Interoperability is about systems working together, not moving.
Elasticity
Elasticity is about scaling.
Resiliency
Resiliency is about surviving failures.

q.q: A hospital runs patient records in a private cloud and bursts its public website to a public cloud during busy periods. Which deployment model is this?
o: Hybrid cloud
Right. Hybrid combines two or more deployment models.
Community cloud
Nothing here is shared with other organizations.
Public cloud
The patient records stay private.
Multi-cloud
One part is private, so it's hybrid.

q.q: Using two public cloud providers for the same workload mainly helps avoid what?
o: Vendor lock-in and single-provider outages
Right. Multi-cloud spreads dependence across providers.
All data residency laws in every country
Laws still apply wherever the data is.
The need for identity and access management
IAM is still needed in each cloud.
The shared responsibility model entirely
Each provider still shares responsibility.

q.q: A company wants to keep full control of the keys used to encrypt its cloud data, even from the provider's staff. Which approach fits BEST?
o: Customer-managed keys in its own HSM (hold your own key)
Right. Keeping keys outside the provider's control limits what the provider can decrypt.
Provider-managed default encryption with keys the provider holds
The provider could still access those keys.
Storing the keys in the same bucket as the encrypted data
Keys next to the data defeat the encryption.
Turning off encryption so the keys don't need managing
That removes protection completely.

q.q: A customer deletes a cloud volume but can't physically wipe the provider's shared disks. What BEST makes the data unrecoverable?
o: Crypto-shredding: destroy the keys that encrypted it
Right. Without the keys, the encrypted data is useless.
Asking the provider to ship the physical disks to the customer
Providers won't hand over shared disks.
Overwriting the volume name with random characters
Renaming doesn't remove data.
Waiting for the provider to reuse the storage eventually
Data could remain readable until it's overwritten.

q.q: Which component is the MOST critical to protect in an IaaS environment because it can create, change and delete every resource?
o: The management plane (console and APIs)
Right. Whoever controls the management plane controls the whole environment.
A single developer's test virtual machine
One VM can't control everything.
The public website's static image files
Static files have limited impact.
The provider's marketing pages about the service
Those aren't part of your environment.

q.q: Why do security teams treat the hypervisor as a high-value target in the cloud?
o: A flaw could expose every VM on the host
Right. The hypervisor isolates tenants, so a flaw there has wide impact.
It stores every customer's billing data and invoices
Billing data isn't held in the hypervisor.
It's the only place where encryption can be turned on
Encryption can be applied at many layers.
It runs inside each customer's guest operating system
It runs beneath the guests.

q.q: In the cloud secure data lifecycle, which phase comes right after Create?
o: Store
Right. Create, Store, Use, Share, Archive, Destroy.
Share
Share comes after Use.
Destroy
Destroy is the last phase.
Archive
Archive comes near the end.

q.q: A team adds security checks like dependency scanning and infrastructure-as-code linting to its deployment pipeline. What approach is this?
o: DevSecOps
Right. Security is built into the DevOps pipeline instead of added at the end.
Waterfall
Waterfall puts testing late.
Shadow IT
Shadow IT is unapproved technology.
A change freeze
A freeze stops changes. It doesn't build security in.

q.q: When designing BC/DR for a cloud app, which analysis tells the team which functions must come back first?
o: Business impact analysis (BIA)
Right. The BIA ranks functions by the harm an outage causes.
A penetration test of the public web front end
Pentests find vulnerabilities.
A code review of the newest feature branch
Code reviews check code quality and flaws.
A capacity forecast for next year's user growth
Capacity planning isn't about recovery order.

q.q: A design adds a second availability zone, encryption, logging and MFA, and estimates their yearly cost against the losses they prevent. What is the team doing?
o: A cost-benefit analysis
Right. Controls should cost less than the risk they reduce.
A data classification exercise for every file
Classification labels data.
A forensic investigation of a past incident
Forensics looks backward at incidents.
A legal hold on all project documents
Legal holds preserve evidence.

q.q: Which ISO/IEC standard gives guidance on information security controls specifically for cloud services?
o: ISO/IEC 27017
Right. 27017 adds cloud-specific guidance to ISO 27002 controls.
ISO/IEC 27701
27701 covers privacy management.
ISO 9001
9001 is about quality, not cloud security.
22301 covers business continuity.

q.q: A customer needs assurance that a provider's crypto module meets U.S. federal requirements. Which validation should it look for?
o: FIPS 140-3
Right. FIPS 140-3 validates cryptographic modules.
SOC 3
A SOC 3 doesn't validate crypto modules.
Common Criteria
Common Criteria evaluates products against protection profiles, not FIPS crypto validation.
PCI DSS
PCI DSS is about cardholder data.

q.q: When comparing providers, why ask for their SOC 2 Type II report instead of Type I?
o: Type II tests controls over a period of time
Right. Type I is a point in time. Type II shows controls kept working.
Type II is shorter and easier for executives to read
Length isn't the difference.
Type I reports are illegal to share with customers
They can be shared under NDA.
Type II covers only financial reporting controls
SOC 1 covers financial reporting.

q.q: A government customer wants a product independently evaluated against a security target and protection profile. Which program fits?
o: Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408)
Right. Common Criteria evaluates IT products against protection profiles.
CSA STAR self-assessment
STAR self-assessment isn't an independent product evaluation.
GDPR certification
That's privacy, not product evaluation.
ITIL certification
ITIL is about IT service processes.

q.q: A SOC uses an AI model to group thousands of alerts and suggest which to investigate first. What is the BIGGEST risk to manage?
o: Its output can be wrong and needs review
Right. AI helps triage, but errors and drift mean humans stay in the loop.
The model will remove the need for any log collection
AI still needs data.
The model makes the SIEM unable to store events
Grouping alerts doesn't stop storage.
The model guarantees zero false negatives from now on
No model guarantees that.

q.q: Which term describes a model's accuracy getting worse over time because real-world data has changed?
o: Model drift
Right. Drift means the model no longer matches the data it sees.
Data sovereignty
Sovereignty is about legal jurisdiction.
Vendor lock-in
Lock-in is a dependency issue.
Crypto-shredding
That's a deletion technique.

q.q: A company deploys an AI chatbot that can call internal APIs. Which threat should the design specifically defend against?
o: Prompt injection that tricks it into misusing those APIs
Right. Crafted input can make the model take unintended actions.
Physical theft of the provider's data center generators
That isn't specific to an AI chatbot.
DNS caching on users' home routers
Unrelated to the chatbot's design.
Expired fonts on the chatbot's web page
Fonts aren't a security threat.

q.q: Which ethics concern applies when an AI model screens job applicants in the cloud?
o: Unfair bias against groups of applicants
Right. Biased training data can lead to discriminatory decisions.
The model using too little storage in the data center
Storage use isn't an ethics issue.
The model's API using HTTPS instead of HTTP
HTTPS is good practice.
Applicants using different web browsers to apply
Browser choice isn't an ethics concern.

q.q: A cloud provider automatically spreads pieces of a customer's stored object across several locations. What is this called?
o: Data dispersion
Right. Dispersion splits and spreads data for resilience.
Data masking
Masking hides values from viewers.
Data classification
Classification labels data.
Data retention
Retention is about how long to keep data.

q.q: Why should a security team map data flows for a cloud app?
o: To see where data travels and where controls are needed
Right. You can't protect data paths you haven't mapped.
To decide what color each server should be on a diagram
Diagram colors aren't the goal.
To replace the need for encryption in transit everywhere
Mapping doesn't replace encryption.
To make the application run faster for remote users
Mapping is about protection, not speed.

q.q: In which lifecycle phase is data MOST exposed to the people and apps processing it?
o: Use
Right. Data is typically decrypted while it's being used.
Archive
Archived data is usually encrypted and idle.
Destroy
Destroyed data is gone.
Store
At rest, it can be encrypted.

q.q: A data breach happened because a storage bucket allowed anonymous public reads. Which control BEST prevents this across the account?
o: An account-wide block on public bucket access
Right. A guardrail at the account level stops any bucket from being made public by mistake.
A strong password on the root account only
Root passwords don't control bucket policies.
Turning on versioning for every bucket in the account
Versioning keeps old copies. It doesn't stop public reads.
Moving the bucket to a region closer to users
Region doesn't affect public access.

q.q: Which storage type is lost when a virtual machine instance is stopped or terminated?
o: Ephemeral storage
Right. Ephemeral (instance) storage lives only as long as the instance.
Object storage
Object storage persists independently.
Persistent block volumes
Persistent block volumes survive stops.
Archive storage
Archive tiers are built to last.

q.q: A database stores records in a managed cloud service. Which threat is MOST specific to its storage layer?
o: Misconfigured access permissions
Right. Misconfigured access is the most common cause of cloud data exposure.
Paper documents left on the office printer overnight
That isn't the cloud storage layer.
A user forgetting their laptop charger at home
Unrelated to storage security.
The office Wi-Fi password being too short for policy
That's a local network issue.

q.q: Which feature helps recover from ransomware that deletes or encrypts objects in cloud storage?
o: Object versioning with immutable (WORM) retention
Right. Locked previous versions can't be deleted or changed by the attacker.
Increasing the bucket's storage size limit
More space doesn't protect existing objects.
Renaming the bucket every week to confuse attackers
Renaming isn't protection.
Turning off access logging to reduce costs
Logging helps investigations.

q.q: A payment app replaces card numbers with random values and keeps the real numbers in a separate secure vault. What is this?
o: Tokenization
Right. Tokens stand in for the data, and only the vault can map them back.
Hashing
Hashes can't be mapped back to the original.
Masking
Masking hides display. It doesn't swap values in storage.
Compression
Compression isn't protection.

q.q: Where should an application's database passwords and API keys be kept in the cloud?
o: In a managed secrets vault, with tight, logged access
Right. Vaults store, rotate and log access to secrets.
Hard-coded in the source code repository for convenience
Secrets in code leak easily.
In a plain-text file on the web server's public folder
Anyone could download it.
In the comments of the deployment pipeline file
Pipeline files are widely readable.

q.q: Which technology watches for sensitive data being uploaded to unapproved cloud apps and blocks it?
o: Data loss prevention (DLP)
Right. DLP inspects content and enforces rules on where it can go.
A load balancer
Load balancers spread traffic.
A content delivery network
CDNs speed delivery.
A hypervisor
Hypervisors isolate VMs.

q.q: A team needs to share realistic customer data with developers without exposing real values. Which technique fits BEST?
o: Data masking or de-identification
Right. Masking keeps the format while hiding the real values.
Giving developers read access to production with a warning
That exposes the real data.
Encrypting the data and also giving developers the key
Then they can read the real data.
Copying production as-is to a test account in another region
The copy still contains real data.

q.q: Which type of data is HARDEST for discovery tools to classify automatically?
o: Unstructured data, like documents and images
Right. Without a fixed schema, tools must analyze content.
Structured data in database tables with named columns
Column names make it easier.
Data in a spreadsheet with a header row for each field
Headers help tools understand it.
Data in a CSV file that follows a published format
A defined format helps discovery.

q.q: JSON and XML files are examples of which kind of data?
o: Semi-structured
Right. They have tags or keys, but no fixed table schema.
Structured
Relational tables are structured.
Unstructured
Tags and keys give them some structure.
Encrypted
Being JSON doesn't mean encrypted.

q.q: Before moving data to the cloud, a team scans file shares to find where personal data lives. Why do this first?
o: You can't protect data you haven't found
Right. Discovery feeds classification and protection.
Cloud providers refuse to store undiscovered data
Providers don't check that.
Discovery makes the migration finish faster
It may add time, but it reduces risk.
Discovery removes the need for encryption later
Data still needs protection.

q.q: A company tags each cloud object with its classification, and access policies read those tags. What does this enable?
o: Controls that follow the data automatically
Right. Tag-based policies apply the right protection wherever the data goes.
Storing every object for free with no billing
Tags don't change cost.
Skipping encryption on any object that has a tag
Tags don't replace encryption.
Letting anyone read objects that are tagged Public or Secret
Policies use tags to restrict, not open.

q.q: Who should decide the classification of a data set?
o: The data owner
Right. Owners understand the data's value and decide its classification.
The cloud provider's support engineer
The provider doesn't own your data.
The developer who built the table
Developers handle data but don't usually own it.
The newest team member
Classification needs authority and context.

q.q: Which document lists what each data type is, where it lives and how it maps to classification levels?
o: A data map or inventory
Right. Data mapping ties data types and locations to their classification.
The firewall rule export from last month
Firewall rules don't describe data.
The incident response contact list
Contacts aren't a data map.
The provider's marketing brochure on storage
Brochures don't describe your data.

q.q: A company wants a confidential report to stay protected even after it's emailed outside, so recipients can view but not print or forward it. Which technology fits?
o: Information rights management (IRM)
Right. IRM controls travel with the file.
A web application firewall
A WAF protects web apps, not files.
Full-disk encryption
Disk encryption doesn't protect the file once sent.
Network access control
Unrelated to file use after sending.

q.q: An employee leaves the company. How can IRM help protect documents she already downloaded?
o: Revoke her rights so the files can't be opened
Right. IRM can revoke access to protected files after the fact.
It can't, because downloaded files are always free to use
IRM is designed for exactly this.
Delete her email account and hope the files are gone
Local copies remain.
Ask her to promise she deleted them
A promise isn't a control.

q.q: What does IRM usually depend on to check who may open a protected file?
o: User identity and issued licenses
Right. IRM verifies the user and their rights before opening the file.
The file's name and size on disk
Names and sizes don't prove identity.
The user's screen resolution and monitor brand
Unrelated to rights.
The time zone set on the computer's clock
Time zone isn't an identity check.

q.q: A lawsuit is expected. What must happen to relevant cloud data, even if its retention period ends?
o: Place it under a legal hold so it isn't deleted
Right. Legal holds override normal deletion schedules.
Delete it on schedule, since policy comes first
Deleting held data can be illegal.
Move it to a personal account for safekeeping
That breaks custody and policy.
Compress it and email it to the lawyers
Copies by email aren't a legal hold.

q.q: Why should a retention policy set BOTH a minimum and a maximum time for data?
o: To meet laws and not keep data too long
Right. Keep data as long as required, then delete it.
So storage bills always stay exactly the same
Cost isn't the main reason.
Because cloud providers require two dates on every file
Providers don't require this.
So data can never be deleted by anyone
The maximum exists to make deletion happen.

q.q: Which storage tier fits records that must be kept for 7 years and are almost never read?
o: An archive tier with retention locks
Right. Archive tiers are cheap for rarely read data, and locks prevent early deletion.
High-performance SSD volumes attached to a VM
That's expensive for idle data.
Ephemeral instance storage on a short-lived VM
That data disappears.
The application's in-memory cache
Caches don't keep data for years.

q.q: Which cloud log is MOST important for tracing who changed a storage bucket's permissions?
o: The control plane audit log (API activity)
Right. API audit logs record who made management changes and when.
The web server's access log for page views
Page views don't show permission changes.
The VM's CPU usage graph
Performance metrics don't show who acted.
The billing invoice for the month
Invoices don't show changes.

q.q: Why send cloud audit logs to a separate account that admins of the main account can't change?
o: An attacker with admin rights could otherwise erase them
Right. Separated, write-protected logs keep the evidence intact.
It makes the logs load faster in the console
Speed isn't the reason.
Providers charge less for logs stored separately
Cost isn't the security reason.
Logs in the main account can't be searched
They can be searched. They just aren't safe there.

q.q: Which property lets an organization prove a specific user downloaded a file and can't credibly deny it?
o: Non-repudiation
Right. Strong identity plus protected logs tie the action to the user.
Elasticity
Elasticity is about scaling.
Data dispersion
Dispersion is about resilience.
Portability
Portability is about moving workloads.

q.q: Attackers slip mislabeled records into a model's training data. Which control helps MOST?
o: Validating and tracking the source of training data
Right. Data validation and provenance help catch poisoning.
Running the model on more powerful GPUs
Hardware doesn't detect bad data.
Making the training data publicly writable for transparency
That invites more poisoning.
Retraining every hour on whatever data arrives
Unchecked retraining spreads poisoned data faster.

q.q: A model was trained on customer records. Why must the model itself be protected like sensitive data?
o: Attacks can sometimes pull training data back out of a model
Right. Model inversion and membership inference can leak training data.
Models are always stored as plain-text customer lists
Models aren't stored that way, but they can still leak.
Cloud providers ban models that used customer data
There's no such general ban.
Protecting the model makes training faster
Protection is about confidentiality.

q.q: Which practice reduces the privacy risk of training an AI model on personal data?
o: Minimizing and de-identifying the data first
Right. Using less personal data, and removing identifiers, lowers the risk.
Collecting every field available in case it helps accuracy
Over-collection increases risk.
Sharing the raw data set with every team that asks
Wider sharing increases exposure.
Keeping the training data forever after the model ships
Indefinite retention adds risk.

q.q: Which component lets one physical server run many isolated virtual machines?
o: The hypervisor
Right. The hypervisor shares hardware among isolated guests.
The content delivery network
CDNs cache content near users.
The identity provider
IdPs handle authentication.
The object storage service
Storage doesn't run VMs.

q.q: In software-defined networking, why must the SDN controller be heavily protected?
o: It programs how traffic flows across the whole network
Right. Control of the controller means control of the network.
It stores every customer's encryption keys in plain text
That isn't the controller's job.
It's the only device that keeps the data center cool
Cooling is physical infrastructure.
It runs the customer's web application code
Apps run on compute, not the controller.

q.q: A customer's IaaS virtual machines can only reach storage through the provider's internal network. Which layer provides this separation for each tenant?
o: Per-tenant virtual networks (VPCs)
Right. Each tenant's virtual network separates its traffic.
The customer's office Wi-Fi password
Office Wi-Fi isn't part of the provider's network.
The web browser used by the admins
Browsers don't separate tenants.
The DNS name of the public website
DNS names don't isolate networks.

q.q: Which compute option shares the host OS kernel between workloads, making kernel patching especially important?
o: Containers
Right. Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel flaw affects them all.
Bare-metal servers
Bare metal doesn't share a kernel with other workloads.
Virtual machines
VMs each run their own kernel.
Developer laptops
Laptops aren't a cloud compute option.

q.q: Which Uptime Institute data center tier is fault tolerant, so it keeps running through any single unplanned equipment failure on independent, fully redundant paths?
o: Tier IV (fault tolerant)
Right. Tier IV survives a single unplanned failure. Tier III only allows planned maintenance without downtime.
Tier I (basic)
Tier I has no redundancy.
Tier II (redundant parts)
Tier II adds parts but still has one path.
Tier III (concurrently maintainable)
Tier III allows planned maintenance without downtime, but it isn't fully fault tolerant.

q.q: Why do data center designs keep hot and cold aisles separate?
o: To cool equipment efficiently and keep it reliable
Right. Separating air flows supports availability by preventing overheating.
To stop people from seeing the server lights
Visibility isn't the purpose.
To keep tenants' data logically separated
Logical separation is done in software.
To meet the encryption requirements of PCI DSS
Airflow has nothing to do with encryption.

q.q: A provider designs its data center so that one tenant's workloads can never reach another's. Which part of design is this?
o: Logical design: tenant separation and access controls
Right. Logical design isolates tenants in software and configuration.
Physical design: fences, guards and mantraps around the site
Physical controls protect the building, not tenant isolation.
Environmental design: power, cooling and fire suppression
That's about keeping equipment running.
Marketing design: choosing the data center's brand colors
Not a security design area.

q.q: Which physical control BEST stops someone from following an authorized person into the server room?
o: A mantrap (access control vestibule)
Right. It lets only one authorized person through at a time.
A sign reminding staff to close the door behind them
A sign is a weak deterrent.
Brighter lights in the parking lot outside
Lighting helps outside, not at the door.
A faster internet connection to the building
Bandwidth doesn't affect physical entry.

q.q: An attacker breaks out of a guest VM and runs code on the host. Which attack is this?
o: VM escape
Right. Escaping the guest can expose every other VM on the host.
VM sprawl
Sprawl is a management problem, not an attack.
Live migration
Migration is a normal operation.
Snapshot restore
Restoring a snapshot is recovery.

q.q: Why can relying on a single cloud provider's region be a risk?
o: A regional outage could take down everything
Right. A single region is a single point of failure.
Regions don't allow encryption of stored data
Every major region supports encryption.
Providers charge double for a single region
Pricing isn't the risk.
Single regions can't run virtual machines
They can.

q.q: Which threat is more likely in a public cloud than on-premises because of shared infrastructure?
o: Side-channel attacks from another tenant on the same hardware
Right. Co-located tenants can sometimes infer data through shared hardware.
Someone stealing a laptop from an employee's car
That happens anywhere.
A power cut at the company's own office
That affects on-premises more.
A user writing their password on a sticky note
That's a user habit, not a cloud risk.

q.q: After assessing cloud infrastructure risks, a team decides to add a second region. Which risk treatment is this?
o: Mitigation
Right. Adding a region reduces the impact of an outage.
Avoidance
They're staying in the cloud.
Transference
Insurance would transfer cost.
Acceptance
They took action.

q.q: Which control BEST protects cloud console access for administrators?
o: Phishing-resistant MFA for every admin account
Right. Admin accounts control everything, so strong MFA is essential.
A shared admin password kept in a team spreadsheet
Shared passwords remove accountability.
Letting admins log in only from personal email accounts
Personal accounts aren't controlled by the company.
Disabling logging so admins aren't slowed down
Logging is needed to track admin actions.

q.q: Which control watches traffic between workloads inside the same virtual network?
o: Security groups or microsegmentation rules
Right. They control east-west traffic between workloads.
The edge firewall at the internet connection only
Edge firewalls see north-south traffic.
The DNS registrar's account lock feature
Registrar locks protect domains.
The provider's physical badge readers
Badges control building entry.

q.q: Why should cloud audit logs be turned on in EVERY region, even unused ones?
o: Attackers may create resources where no one is looking
Right. Unused regions are a favorite place to hide.
Providers require logs in every region by law
There's no such general law.
Logs in unused regions make the console faster
Logging doesn't affect speed.
Unused regions can't be logged anyway
They can, and should be.

q.q: A cloud app must lose no more than 5 minutes of data and be back within 1 hour. Which values are these?
o: RPO 5 minutes, RTO 1 hour
Right. RPO is data loss in time. RTO is time to recover.
RTO 5 minutes, RPO 1 hour
The labels are reversed.
MTBF 5 minutes, MTTR 1 hour
Those measure failure rate and repair time.
SLA 5 minutes, MSA 1 hour
Those are contract documents.

q.q: Which DR approach keeps only the core pieces, like a replicated database, running in another region and starts the app servers when disaster strikes?
o: Pilot light
Right. Only the core runs. A warm standby would keep a smaller full copy running.
Backup and restore
That's slower and has nothing running.
Active-active
That's full capacity in both places.
Warm standby (a smaller full copy)
Warm standby keeps a scaled-down but complete copy running, not just the core.

q.q: Why should DR plans for cloud apps be tested regularly?
o: Constant change can break an untested plan
Right. Frequent change means frequent testing.
Providers delete DR plans that aren't tested
Providers don't manage your plans.
Testing replaces the need for backups
Backups are still needed.
Testing is only needed for on-premises systems
Cloud systems need testing too.

q.q: A company stores its cloud backups in the same account as production. What risk does this create?
o: An attacker who takes the account can destroy both
Right. Backups should be isolated, such as in a separate account with locks.
The backups will restore too quickly
Speed isn't the risk.
The backups can't be encrypted in the same account
They can be encrypted.
Providers won't bill for backups in the same account
Billing isn't the risk.

q.q: During a regional outage, who decides to declare a disaster and start failover?
o: The people named in the BC/DR plan
Right. The plan names who can declare a disaster, so no time is lost.
Any user who notices the site is slow
Users don't trigger DR.
The cloud provider's sales representative
The provider doesn't run your DR decisions.
Whoever is first to post about it online
DR decisions follow the plan.

q.q: Which test fails a cloud workload over to the DR region for real, then back?
o: A full failover test
Right. It proves the DR setup actually works.
A tabletop exercise
Tabletops are discussions only.
A checklist review
That checks the document, not the systems.
A walk-through
A walk-through steps through the plan without failing over.

q.q: Which control helps detect a cloud account being used to mine cryptocurrency?
o: Alerts on unusual spending and compute usage
Right. Sudden cost or usage spikes are a common sign of cryptojacking.
A stronger password on the office printer
Unrelated to cloud abuse.
Turning off all billing notifications
That hides the warning signs.
Moving all workloads to one availability zone
That doesn't detect abuse.

q.q: Which part of the cloud lets admins create, change and delete resources through a web console, CLI and APIs?
o: The management plane
Right. It's the most powerful part of the environment and needs the strongest protection.
The data plane
The data plane moves workload traffic.
The guest OS
Guests run workloads, not the cloud.
The facility cooling system
Cooling is environmental infrastructure.

q.q: Which resource lists the most critical web application security risks and is widely used in developer training?
o: The OWASP Top 10
Right. It's a common starting point for app security awareness.
The ITIL service catalog
ITIL is about IT service management.
ISO 9001
That's about quality management.
FIPS 199
FIPS 199 rates impact levels.

q.q: Developers keep exposing cloud storage keys in public code repositories. What training change helps MOST?
o: Teach secrets handling, plus pre-commit secret scanning
Right. Training plus tooling stops secrets before they're pushed.
Tell them to make repositories private and hope for the best
Private repos still leak keys to many people.
Ban developers from using the cloud entirely
That stops the business.
Ask them to use shorter keys that are easier to hide
Shorter keys are weaker and still exposed.

q.q: Which is a common cloud development pitfall that training should cover?
o: Assuming the provider secures everything, including app settings
Right. Customers still own app security under shared responsibility.
Using HTTPS for every API endpoint
That's good practice.
Encrypting sensitive data at rest
That's good practice.
Writing unit tests for new features
That's good practice.

q.q: In which SDLC phase should security requirements be defined?
o: Requirements, at the start
Right. Early requirements are cheaper than late fixes.
Only after the app is in production
Fixes after release cost much more.
During decommissioning of the old system
That's the end of the life cycle.
Only during the final penetration test
Testing checks requirements, it doesn't set them.

q.q: How does security fit into an Agile process with two-week sprints?
o: Build security tasks and checks into every sprint
Right. Security is part of each iteration, not a final gate.
Save all security work for one sprint at the end of the year
Problems pile up.
Skip security because Agile moves too fast
Speed doesn't remove the need.
Let only the security team write user stories
Security works with the whole team.

q.q: Which business requirement should drive security decisions for a cloud app?
o: Data sensitivity and the app's mission role
Right. What the app does and handles shapes its security needs.
Which programming language the newest developer prefers
Preferences don't drive security.
The color scheme chosen by the design team
Visual design isn't a security driver.
How many lines of code the app has
Size alone doesn't set requirements.

q.q: Before coding a new API, a team lists who might attack it and how, using STRIDE. What is this?
o: Threat modeling
Right. STRIDE helps find spoofing, tampering and other threats early.
Penetration testing
Pentesting comes after the API exists.
Load testing
Load tests measure performance.
Change management
That controls changes to running systems.

q.q: Which secure coding practice BEST prevents SQL injection?
o: Parameterized queries
Right. Parameters keep user input from being run as SQL.
Hiding error messages
Hidden errors don't stop injection.
A longer database password
Password length doesn't stop injection.
A faster database server
Speed doesn't stop injection.

q.q: Why should infrastructure-as-code templates go through the same review as application code?
o: A bad template can misconfigure many resources at once
Right. IaC mistakes spread quickly, so they need review and scanning.
Templates are never deployed to production
They're often how production is built.
Reviewing templates makes the cloud cheaper
Cost isn't the main reason.
Templates can't contain security settings
They're full of security settings.

q.q: Which test analyzes source code for flaws without running it?
o: Static application security testing (SAST)
Right. SAST reviews code before it runs.
Dynamic application security testing against a live app
DAST tests the running app.
A disaster recovery failover test
That tests recovery.
A user acceptance test of the new screens
UAT checks that features meet needs.

q.q: Testers write cases for how an attacker might misuse a feature, like changing an order's price. What are these?
o: Abuse (misuse) cases
Right. Abuse cases test how a feature could be misused.
Use cases
Use cases cover normal use.
Load test cases
Those are performance tests.
Accessibility cases
Those check accessibility.

q.q: Where should automated security tests run so problems are caught before release?
o: In the CI/CD pipeline, with failing builds blocked
Right. Pipeline gates stop vulnerable code from shipping.
Only on production after users complain
That's far too late.
On a developer's laptop once a year
Too rare and inconsistent.
Nowhere, since QA testers check everything manually
Manual QA alone misses a lot.

q.q: A team wants to know every open-source library inside its container images. Which artifact helps MOST?
o: A software bill of materials (SBOM)
Right. An SBOM lists components so vulnerable ones can be found.
A list of the team members' email addresses
That doesn't describe the software.
The container's CPU and memory settings
Resources don't list libraries.
The cloud invoice for the container service
Invoices don't list components.

q.q: Which practice reduces the risk of a tampered third-party package reaching production?
o: Pin versions and verify signatures or checksums
Right. Verification confirms the package is the one the publisher released.
Always pull the newest version automatically with no checks
Unchecked updates can bring in tampered code.
Copy packages from random mirrors to save time
Untrusted mirrors raise the risk.
Disable dependency scanning to speed up builds
Scanning catches known bad packages.

q.q: A partner API returns data to your cloud app. How should your app treat that data?
o: Validate it like any untrusted input
Right. Data from third-party APIs can be malicious or malformed.
Trust it fully, because it comes from a partner
Partners can be compromised too.
Store it without checks, since APIs can't send bad data
APIs can send bad data.
Display it directly in HTML without encoding
That invites cross-site scripting.

q.q: Which component inspects HTTP requests to a cloud web app and blocks attacks like SQL injection and XSS?
o: A web application firewall (WAF)
Right. A WAF filters application-layer attacks.
A network load balancer working at layer 4
Layer 4 balancers don't inspect HTTP content.
A VPN concentrator for remote staff
VPNs encrypt remote access.
An object storage lifecycle rule
Lifecycle rules move or delete objects.

q.q: A company exposes many microservices to partners. Which component gives one place to enforce authentication, rate limits and logging for them?
o: An API gateway
Right. Gateways centralize API security controls.
A DNS server
DNS doesn't enforce API policy.
A shared key spreadsheet
That's not an enforcement point, and it's insecure.
A bigger database
Database size doesn't secure APIs.

q.q: Untrusted user-uploaded files are opened in an isolated environment that can't reach anything else. What is this?
o: Sandboxing
Right. A sandbox limits what untrusted code or content can affect.
Tokenization
Tokenization replaces sensitive data values.
Federation
Federation is about identity trust.
Data dispersion
Dispersion spreads data for resilience.

q.q: Employees log in to many SaaS apps using their company identity provider. Which technology lets the apps trust those logins?
o: Federation using SAML or OpenID Connect
Right. Federation lets apps accept the IdP's authentication.
A separate password for each app stored in a notebook
That's the problem federation solves.
A shared generic account for each department
Shared accounts break accountability.
Port forwarding on the office router
That's a network setting.

q.q: A company wants visibility and control over which cloud apps employees use, including unapproved ones. Which tool fits?
o: A cloud access security broker (CASB)
Right. A CASB finds shadow IT and enforces cloud usage policies.
A hardware security module for key storage
HSMs protect keys.
A load balancer in front of the intranet
Load balancers spread traffic.
A tape library for long-term backups
Tapes store backups.

q.q: A cloud workload needs to read one storage bucket. What is the BEST way to give it access?
o: A role with read access to that bucket only
Right. Workload identities with least privilege avoid long-lived keys.
An admin user's access keys pasted into the app's config
Long-lived admin keys are dangerous if leaked.
Making the bucket public so the workload can read it
That exposes the data to everyone.
The root account's credentials for simplicity
Root should never be used for apps.

q.q: Which approach makes new cloud servers secure by default every time they're built?
o: Hardened golden images built from a secure baseline
Right. Every server starts from the same hardened, tested image.
Letting each admin configure servers however they like
That leads to inconsistent, weak setups.
Using the vendor's default image without changes
Defaults are often not hardened.
Building servers by hand from a printed checklist
Manual builds drift and are error-prone.

q.q: What should be removed from a VM image before it's used in production?
o: Unneeded services, default accounts and test tools
Right. Removing extras shrinks the attack surface.
The security agent and logging configuration
Those should stay.
The OS patches applied during the build
Patches should stay.
The host-based firewall rules
The firewall should stay.

q.q: Which hardware feature helps verify that a cloud server booted with trusted, unmodified firmware and OS?
o: Secure boot with a TPM (measured boot)
Right. It checks each boot stage against trusted values.
A larger hard drive for the system volume
Disk size doesn't verify boot integrity.
A faster network card in the server
Network speed isn't boot integrity.
A second monitor attached to the host
Monitors don't verify anything.

q.q: How should patches be applied to a fleet of cloud servers built from images?
o: Rebuild from a patched, tested image
Right. Immutable infrastructure replaces servers instead of patching them in place.
Log in to each server by hand and patch it live
That's slow and causes drift.
Never patch, since cloud providers patch guest OSs
In IaaS, the customer patches the guest OS.
Patch only the servers that users complain about
Unpatched servers stay exposed.

q.q: Two web servers sit behind a load balancer across two availability zones. Which goal does this mainly support?
o: High availability
Right. If one zone or server fails, the other keeps serving.
Data classification
Classification labels data.
Non-repudiation
That's about proving who did something.
Data sovereignty
That's about where data is legally held.

q.q: Why should backups in the cloud be restore-tested regularly?
o: A backup that can't be restored is worthless
Right. Testing proves recovery works.
Restore tests make backups smaller
Testing doesn't change size.
Providers delete untested backups automatically
They don't.
Testing replaces the need for encryption of backups
Backups still need encryption.

q.q: Which monitoring signal MOST likely shows a guest OS needs attention?
o: Failed logins and surprise admin accounts
Right. Those point to possible compromise.
The server's hostname being long
Name length isn't a signal.
Normal CPU use during business hours
That's expected.
A scheduled backup finishing on time
That's healthy.

q.q: Which framework focuses on IT service management processes like incident, problem and change management?
o: ITIL
Right. ITIL describes best practices for running IT services.
FIPS 140-3
That validates crypto modules.
OWASP ASVS
ASVS verifies app security.
GDPR
GDPR is a privacy law.

q.q: Which ISO/IEC standard specifies requirements for a service management system?
o: ISO/IEC 20000-1
Right. 20000-1 covers IT service management systems.
ISO/IEC 27018
27018 covers protecting PII in public cloud.
ISO/IEC 15408
15408 is for product evaluation.
14001 is environmental.

q.q: A cloud team wants prioritized, practical safeguards it can apply right away. Which set fits BEST?
o: The CIS Critical Security Controls
Right. The CIS Controls are a prioritized list of safeguards.
The COBIT governance framework for boards
COBIT is about IT governance.
The FedRAMP authorization process for agencies
That's an authorization program.
SOC 1 reports on financial controls
SOC 1 is about financial reporting.

q.q: Why is forensic collection harder in a public cloud than on-premises?
o: The customer doesn't control the physical hardware
Right. You often rely on snapshots, logs and the provider's cooperation.
Cloud data can't ever be copied for evidence
Snapshots and exports are possible.
Forensics is illegal in public clouds
It isn't illegal.
Cloud servers don't keep any logs at all
Cloud services produce many logs.

q.q: A compromised cloud VM must be investigated. What should the responder capture FIRST?
o: Memory and a disk snapshot, before shutting it down
Right. Volatile memory is lost at shutdown, so capture it first.
Nothing, just terminate the VM right away
Terminating destroys evidence.
Only a screenshot of the console login page
That captures almost nothing useful.
The VM's monthly bill
Billing data isn't the key evidence.

q.q: How should a contract help with cloud forensics BEFORE an incident happens?
o: Agree on evidence and log access up front
Right. Agreeing in advance avoids delays during an investigation.
Ban all forensic activity in the provider's data center
That would block investigations.
Require the provider to delete logs every day
That destroys evidence.
Leave forensics out, since it's rarely needed
When it's needed, it's needed fast.

q.q: During a cloud data breach, who should the communication plan say speaks to regulators?
o: The designated legal or compliance contact
Right. Regulator communication must be accurate and follow legal rules.
Any engineer who has details of the incident
Unplanned statements can cause legal problems.
The provider's sales team on the customer's behalf
The customer owns its regulatory duties.
Whoever posts first on social media
That's not a plan.

q.q: Why should a cloud customer know how its provider will notify it of security incidents?
o: The customer may have its own deadlines to notify others
Right. Laws like GDPR set deadlines the customer must meet.
Providers never have incidents
They do.
Notifications replace the customer's own monitoring
Customers still need their own monitoring.
It lowers the monthly bill
Notification terms don't change cost.

q.q: Which party should be told about a planned maintenance window that will affect a shared service?
o: Customers and partners who depend on it
Right. Advance notice lets them plan around the outage.
Only the newest engineer on the team
Dependents need to know.
Nobody, to avoid worrying anyone
Surprise outages hurt trust.
Competitors, so they can prepare
Competitors don't need notice.

q.q: A SOC collects cloud API logs, VPC flow logs and identity logs in one place and correlates them. What tool is this?
o: A SIEM
Right. A SIEM centralizes and correlates security events.
A CDN
CDNs deliver content.
A code repository
Repos store code.
A password manager
That stores credentials.

q.q: Before running a penetration test against its IaaS workloads, what should the customer check?
o: The provider's testing policy and any notice it requires
Right. Providers set rules for testing on their platforms.
Nothing, since the customer owns everything in the cloud
The provider owns the underlying platform.
Whether other tenants mind being tested too
Other tenants are never in scope.
Whether the test can be run without logging
Logging should stay on.

q.q: A vulnerability scan finds a critical flaw in a public-facing cloud API. Which process should the fix go through?
o: Change management, with emergency approval if needed
Right. Even urgent fixes are tracked and approved.
Deploy directly to production with no record
Unrecorded changes create new risks.
Wait for the next yearly release
Critical exposed flaws can't wait.
Ask users to avoid the API until next year
That's not a fix.

q.q: Which practice helps a cloud team make sure it has enough resources before a big seasonal spike?
o: Capacity management with load testing and auto-scaling
Right. Planning capacity protects availability.
Turning off monitoring during the spike
Monitoring is most important then.
Reducing the number of servers just before the spike
That causes outages.
Disabling auto-scaling to control costs
That risks running out of capacity.

q.q: A company's cloud data is stored in a country whose laws let the government demand access. Which risk is this?
o: Conflicting laws across jurisdictions
Right. Data in another country falls under that country's laws.
Model drift in an AI system
Unrelated to legal jurisdiction.
VM sprawl in the account
That's a management issue.
Hypervisor escape on shared hosts
That's a technical attack.

q.q: A lawsuit requires a company to produce relevant emails stored in a SaaS service. What process is this?
o: eDiscovery
Right. eDiscovery finds and produces electronic information for legal cases.
Data classification
Classification labels data.
Penetration testing
That tests security.
Capacity planning
That's about resources.

q.q: Why must cloud contracts address where data may be stored?
o: Some laws restrict moving data out of the country
Right. Data localization laws can limit storage locations.
Providers can only store data on one continent
Providers have many regions.
Storage location doesn't affect any legal duties
It often does.
Location only matters for performance
It also matters legally.

q.q: Under GDPR, a company that decides why and how personal data is processed in the cloud is called what?
o: The controller
Right. The controller decides the purposes and means of processing.
The processor
The processor acts on the controller's behalf.
The data subject
That's the individual.
The supervisory authority
That's the regulator.

q.q: A cloud provider stores and processes personal data only on the customer's instructions. Under GDPR, what is the provider?
o: A processor
Right. Processors act on the controller's documented instructions.
The controller of the data
The customer decides why and how, so it's the controller.
The data protection authority
That's the regulator.
The data subject
That's the person the data is about.

q.q: Before launching a cloud service that processes lots of personal data, what should the company perform?
o: A privacy impact assessment (or DPIA)
Right. It identifies and reduces privacy risks before launch.
A load test of the login page
That checks performance.
A logo redesign for the service
Unrelated to privacy.
A firewall rule cleanup
Useful, but not a privacy assessment.

q.q: What is the difference between contractual and regulated private data?
o: Contracts protect some data; laws protect other data
Right. Contractual data is protected by agreement, and regulated data by law.
Regulated data is never personal
Regulated data is often personal.
Contractual data has no protection at all
The contract is the protection.
They're the same thing
They come from different sources of obligation.

q.q: A customer wants a provider report it can share publicly on its website about the provider's controls. Which report fits?
o: SOC 3
Right. SOC 3 is a general-use summary report.
SOC 2 Type II
SOC 2 is restricted use.
SOC 1
SOC 1 isn't for public sharing or security.
An internal audit memo
Internal memos aren't independent reports.

q.q: A customer's audit team wants to inspect a public cloud provider's data center in person. What usually happens instead?
o: It relies on independent audit reports
Right. Providers share third-party audit results because they can't host every customer's auditors.
The provider gives every customer unlimited site access
That isn't practical or secure.
The audit is skipped and the provider is trusted
Assurance still comes from reports.
The customer hires the provider's staff to audit themselves
That isn't independent.

q.q: An auditor compares a company's current cloud controls against a target framework to find missing pieces. What is this?
o: A gap analysis
Right. It shows what's missing compared with the target.
A penetration test
That tests exploitability.
A load test
That tests capacity.
Data classification
That labels data.

q.q: Why might a provider's SOC 2 report have limited value for a customer's audit?
o: Its scope may not cover the services the customer uses
Right. Always check the report's scope and period.
SOC 2 reports are never independent
They're done by independent auditors.
SOC 2 reports can't mention security
Security is a core SOC 2 criterion.
SOC 2 reports are written by customers
Independent auditors write them.

q.q: Why does moving to the cloud change enterprise risk management?
o: Some risks now depend on the provider's controls
Right. The organization must assess and monitor the provider's risk environment.
The cloud removes all of the organization's risk
Risk remains, it just shifts.
Risk management is no longer needed in the cloud
It's still needed.
Providers take legal responsibility for all customer data
Customers keep accountability for their data.

q.q: Which metric would BEST tell leadership whether cloud risk is under control?
o: Percent of critical misconfigurations fixed on time
Right. It shows whether the biggest risks are being handled.
Number of cloud accounts created this year
Counting accounts doesn't measure risk.
The number of emails sent by the cloud team
Activity isn't risk.
The total size of the logs collected
Volume isn't risk.

q.q: A company decides its tolerance for cloud outages is low, so it pays for multi-region design. Which concept guided the decision?
o: Risk appetite
Right. How much risk leadership will accept drives how much it invests.
Data dispersion
Dispersion is a storage technique.
eDiscovery
That's a legal process.
Tokenization
That replaces sensitive values.

q.q: Which contract document defines measurable targets like 99.9% uptime and the credits paid if they're missed?
o: The service level agreement (SLA)
Right. SLAs set service targets and remedies.
The statement of work (SOW)
A SOW describes specific project work.
The non-disclosure agreement (NDA)
An NDA protects confidential information.
The acceptable use policy (AUP)
An AUP governs employee behavior.

q.q: Why should a cloud contract include exit terms?
o: So data is returned and deleted at the end
Right. Exit terms prevent lock-in and data left behind.
So the provider can keep the data as long as it likes
That's the risk exit terms address.
Exit terms make the service run faster
They don't affect performance.
They're only needed for on-premises contracts
Cloud contracts need them most.

q.q: A customer wants the contractual right to verify the provider's controls. Which clause provides this?
o: A right-to-audit clause
Right. It lets the customer or its auditors assess the provider, often through reports.
A force majeure clause
That excuses performance in disasters.
A non-compete clause
That limits competition.
A severability clause
That keeps the contract valid if one part fails.

q.q: A company signs one master agreement with a provider and then separate documents for each project's work. What are those per-project documents?
o: Statements of work (SOWs)
Right. SOWs define the work under the master service agreement.
Service level agreements
SLAs set performance targets.
Privacy notices
Those inform individuals.
Security assessment reports
Those record assessment results.

q.title: Who manages what in each service model
q.scenario: For each layer, pick who is mainly responsible in the named service model.

rows.req: IaaS: patching the guest operating system.
rows.why: In IaaS the customer runs the OS.

rows.req: PaaS: patching the runtime and OS under the app.
rows.why: In PaaS the provider manages the platform.

rows.req: SaaS: deciding which users can access the app and its data.
rows.why: Identity and data access always stay with the customer.

rows.req: Any model: physical security of the data center.
IaaS: network security, with provider network plus customer firewall rules.
rows.why: The provider secures the underlying network, and the customer configures its own rules.

q.title: Pick the data protection technique
q.scenario: Five needs. Pick the technique that fits each one best.

rows.req: Replace card numbers in an app with values that only a secure vault can map back.
rows.why: Tokenization swaps data for tokens kept in a vault.

rows.req: Show support agents only the last four digits of an account number.
rows.why: Masking hides part of the value on screen.

rows.req: Check that a downloaded file matches the published fingerprint.
Make deleted data in a shared cloud unreadable when disks can't be wiped.
rows.why: Destroying the keys makes the encrypted data useless.

rows.req: Protect a database at rest so a stolen copy can't be read.
rows.why: Encryption at rest protects stolen copies.

q.title: Choose the audit report
q.scenario: Four needs. Pick the report or assessment that fits each one. Two options are distractors.

items.text: Your auditors need assurance about the provider's controls over financial reporting.
items.why: SOC 1 covers controls relevant to financial reporting.

items.text: You need evidence that security controls worked over the past 12 months.
items.why: Type II tests operating effectiveness over a period.

items.text: Marketing wants a provider report it can post publicly.
You only need to know if controls were designed properly on one date.
items.why: Type I covers design at a point in time.

q.title: Pick the security test
q.scenario: Five testing needs in a cloud app's pipeline. Pick the test that fits each. Two options are distractors.

items.text: Find SQL injection by reading the source code before it runs.
items.why: Static analysis reviews code without running it.

items.text: Probe the running staging site for XSS from the outside.
items.why: Dynamic testing attacks the running app.

items.text: Find known-vulnerable open-source libraries in the build.
Check whether a user can change another user's order total.
items.why: Abuse cases test how features can be misused.

items.text: Catch a storage bucket set to public in a Terraform template.
items.why: IaC scanning finds misconfigurations before deployment.

q.title: Choose the DR strategy
q.scenario: Four cloud workloads. Pick the DR approach that best fits each one's recovery needs and budget.

rows.req: Internal wiki. Down for a day is fine; lowest cost wins.
rows.why: Restoring from backups is cheapest and slowest.

rows.req: Order system. Core database must replicate; app servers can start in about an hour.
rows.why: A pilot light keeps the core running and scales the rest up.

rows.req: Customer portal. A scaled-down copy runs all the time and must take over within minutes.
rows.why: Warm standby runs a smaller full copy that scales up fast.

rows.req: Payment API. No noticeable downtime allowed, cost is secondary.
rows.why: Active-active serves from both regions at once.

q.title: Match the contract term
q.scenario: Four contract needs. Pick the document or clause that covers each one. Two options are distractors.

items.text: 99.95% uptime target with service credits if it's missed.
items.why: SLAs define measurable service levels and remedies.

items.text: The overall legal terms that govern every future project with the provider.
items.why: The master service agreement sets the overall terms.

items.text: The tasks, deliverables and dates for one migration project.
items.why: A statement of work describes one project's work.

items.text: The customer can review the provider's controls or its audit reports.
items.why: A right-to-audit clause gives the customer that ability.
